action_name: Shift short-distance freight transportation to cargo bikes
description: Transporting freight short distances, whether it’s last-mile delivery or movement of goods around a farmers’ market, can often be carried out on cargo bikes.

action_name: Increase urban density
description:
Increasing urban density is a key component of city planning to reduce the amount of energy required for travel, for building heating and cooling, and for all types of infrastructure from electricity network expansion to water and wastewater piping, to road networks, transit services, street lighting, fire hydrants, and fire rescue services. 
Communities in which residents are closer together, closer to their places of employment, schools, and the services they access regularly can travel to more of their destinations on bikes, walking or by transit. This in turn reduces the need for large-scale roadways to handle single-occupant vehicles. 
Similarly, buildings with more shared walls and fewer external walls are more energy efficient. This means that row housing is easier to make more energy efficient than single-family housing, and apartment complexes are easier to make more energy efficient than row housing.  
There are many ways to increase urban density. Municipalities can leverage their zoning bylaws to require and incentivize denser housing or commercial developments in selected zones, as well as 'mixed-use' developments  in which there are dwellings, services and businesses all within the same building or directly adjacent to each other. Municipalities can also require active transportation infrastructure and limit the amount of parking for vehicles, to simultaneously incentivize active transportation and discourage vehicle use, particularly for short trips.

action_name: Add green roofs to new buildings to reduce the energy required to cool the building.
description:
What are green roofs?
A green roof or living roof is a roof of a building that is partially or completely covered with vegetation and a growing medium, planted over a waterproofing membrane. It may also include additional layers such as a root barrier and drainage and irrigation systems.
Why do we include this action? 
Installing green roofs provides many benefits including: 
- Creating a natural buffer that insulates and primarily cools the building's interior, reducing the energy required to cool the space with technology. A simple sedum roof on a building in Canada provides energy savings (for cooling) of 75% in a single-storey building and 29% in a 2-storey building.
- Sequestering CO2 in the vegetation growth on the roof, removes GHGs from the atmosphere. A simple sedum roof on a building in Canada sequesters 13.74 kg / m2 / year.
- Extending the life expectancy of the roof surface below the green roof by moderating the temperature variation it is exposed to.
- Increasing habitat for insects and birds, supporting an increase in biodiversity.
- Absorbing rainfall during storm events, reducing the volume of water reaching stormwater infrastructure.
- Absorption of other air pollutants by the rooftop vegetation, producing better outdoor quality around the building.

action_name: Reduce average dwelling size, and increase the number of multi-family dwellings while reducing the number of single family dwellings, for new residential construction
description:
The most difficult wall of any building to make energy-efficient is an exterior wall, because of the temperature gradient between outside and inside. For the same reason, multi-unit residential buildings are more energy-efficient ways to house people than to build many single-family homes.

Sinilarly, decreasing the average size of homes also reduces the amount of energy required to heat and cool a community’s per capita living space.

action_name: Remove buildings that cannot be retrofit, refurbished or repurposed
description: If buildings exist that cannot be renovated sufficiently, they should be taken down. As much as possible the components of the building should be re-used. Those that cannot be re-used should be broken down into their constituent parts to become materials to be used for other manufacturing.

action_name: Retrofit non-residential buildings to improve energy efficiency and decrease energy use
description: See Retrofit existing buildings to reduce energy use and improve energy efficiency for details.

action_name: Install faucet aerators
Improve energy efficiency of appliances and other plug load
description:
Although SSG rarely models this action, it is important that communities support replacing appliances with energy-efficient models. This is part of the overall need to reduce per-household energy consumption before switching everything to electricity. This is also an area that national standards are already addressing, so it isn't as high a priority as other actions. 
Because it isn’t normally included in SSG’s modelling, and is often part of existing programs, it has not been identified as 'Not Generally Included'. However, it can still be discussed with a client during projects or included in Climate Action Plans, , as requiring certain standards can be included in corporate buildings standards, new building standards, affordable housing standards, etc.		
The most commonly-used reference in North America for identifying high-efficiency appliances is the American ENERGY STAR program (https://www.energystar.gov/?s=mega).

action_name: Manage energy distribution more efficiently to reduce overall consumption
description:
'Smart technologies' can be used to reduce overall energy consumption. For example, smart home thermostats and building management controls allow you to program heating and air-conditioning equipment to keep the building at a desired temperature only during specific hours, and to optimize its energy use at other times. Lighting such as outdoor illuminated signs can also be programmed to operate only at specific times. And the use of presence and brightness detectors can optimize lighting and reduce overall energy demand. 
Technologies can also allow:
- Heat extracted from an ice arena in a recreation centre to be pumped over to a swimming pool within the same building, avoiding the waste that occurs if you generate heat for the pool while simultaneously blowing heat out of the ice arena. 
- Communities to optimize their overall energy consumption by diverting waste heat from one building (an industrial facility for example) to another (perhaps a commercial facility) through a district energy system.
- Groups of buildings to store excess renewable energy when a system is generating more than is required, and store it for use later, rather than releasing it and having to draw power from the grid later.

action_name: Increase pumping efficiency
description: Water and wastewater treatment are often the single largest consumers of energy within the portfolio a city’s corporately owned facilities. At the same time, they are often older, using much less efficient pumps than are available now, and wasting energy in a multitude of ways. The specific changes required will vary by facility and require detailed, engineering-level analyses. But for our modelling, we can assume simplified expressions of improvements such as, “Overall efficiency of water pumping is improved by 5% by 2035.” (That’s just an example.) This action should only be used if we have enough detail about the whole water treatment system to be able to control only the pump portion of the facility’s total energy use.

description: This action focuses on the energy efficiency gains from having a central system for multiple systems, regardless of the fuel source. It should be used in combination with "Establish, expand (or switch fuel to) zero emissions fueled district energy systems"

action_name: Decarbonize electricity
description:
What does this mean?
Decarbonizing electricity means switching the fuel sources for electricity production from fossil fuels to small-scale solar PV, onshore wind, offshore wind, and utility-scale solar, as well as potentially nuclear power. 
What is the current trend? 
U.S.
In 1990, the use of coal to produce electricity peaked, and since 2000 there has been a sharp increase in the adoption of renewables in the U.S. In 2024 for the first time power generation from wind and solar (17% nationally) was greater than coal (15%). 
Canada
Since 2010, at least 62% of Canada's electricity has been generated by hydro power. In 2023, more than 8% of Canada's total electricity demand was met with wind or solar power. (Source: https://renewablesassociation.ca/by-the-numbers/).  
What is required?
Globally, we need 11,000 GW of renewable energy by 2030. This represented a tripling of the global renewable energy capacity that existed in 2023 when the Tripling Renewable Capacity Pledge was created at COP28. 
Global renewable capacity additions reached almost 560 GW in 2023, an unprecedented 64% year-over-year increase from 2022. This is in line with the annual pace needed to reach nearly 8 000 GW of installed capacity by 2030, a total that matches countries’ current policies, plans and estimates. However China was by far the biggest contributor, installing almost 350 GW of that global total. The rest of the world - especially the European Union, the U.S. and India - need to accelerate their avg annual growth of renewables by at least 36% to achieve this target. (Source: https://www.iea.org/reports/cop28-tripling-renewable-capacity-pledge/executive-summary)

action_name: Produce electricity from hydrological energy
description:
Hydro power actions can include:
- 'Run of river' power which involves installing turbines on rivers (with or without dam infrastructure). This is increasingly being used as a base, steady power source especially in remote communities, even with small rivers.
- Adding power generation to dams that are currently used only for water management.
- Tidal power.
- Wave power.
Hydro is an excellent 'dispatchable' power source, meaning it can produce power almost immediately, any time, on demand.

action_name: Install solar PV system capacity on rooftops, balconies, within building-cladding, and as shade awnings.
description:
Rooftop Solar PV
Rooftop solar PV is generally installed on south-facing (or to a lesser extent, east and west-facing) areas of a building roof that do not receive a significant amount of shade. Optimally, they are positioned at an angle equal to the location's latitude.
The amount of energy produced depends on the amount of solar irradiation received in the location where the system is installed. E.g. a system installed in Ontario receives an avg of 1,166 'equivalent full sunlight hours' whereas one installed in BC receives 1,004 'equivalent full sunlight hours'. As a result, on average a solar system installed in Ontario will produce more power than one of the same size installed in BC. 
Rooftop solar PV only provides energy when the sun is shining. It provides more energy the closer the suns rays are to perpendicular to the panel. So these systems will provide less energy during seasons when the sun is lower in the sky.
Many systems generate more than the building they are installed on needs on sunny summer days. This excess energy can be stored in batteries onsite to be used later, or it can be provided back to the grid. A net-metering agreement refers to the situation in which a building with a solar system remains connected to the grid so that it can provide excess production back into the grid, and also so that when the solar system isn't producing power, the building can draw from the grid. 
Plug-in Balcony Solar Panels
These are small, bery inexpensive solar panels that can be hung over a balcony a plugged into an ordinary outlet in the house where theybegin providing power to the house. They don’t feed back into the grid. In the US, they can cost $2000, and pay for themselves in savings within 3 years. They’re most popular in Germany where there are now more than 1.2 million systems operating.

action_name: Establish, expand, or switch fuel to zero emissions fueled district energy systems
description:
What is it? District energy is one of the oldest concepts about energy in history, dating back at least to the ancient Romans. It refers simply to connecting multiple buildings to a single source of heating and cooling. That source may be a natural gas furnace (which in 2023 the majority of the systems still were), industrial-scale heat pumps, geothermal wells, deep lakes, waste heat from underground sewer systems, etc. and distributing that heat or cooling via water or steam flowing through underground pipes. 
What's the benefit? The advantages of district energy include: 
- Efficiency and economies of scale: Building heating and cooling for many buildings are controlled by just one system. This means you only need to pay for and perform maintenance on one system.
- Less energy is wasted because there are more opportunities to make smart use of the energy within a number of buildings. That is, within a district energy system, energy can be moved around among buildings, so that if one area needs to be cooled off and another heated, you can simply move the heat away from one towards the other, rather than expending energy to blow cool air outdoors from one, and then burning fuel to heat the other. 
- When it comes to decarbonization, you 'only' need to upgrade the one, large central system and the benefits flow seamlessly through the same steam or water-filled pipes to hundreds or even thousands of people in work or home settings, eliminating many more emissions from a single upgrade initiative than if you had to do each building separately. 
- You can also improvement efficiency by adding combined heat and power systems to take excess heat from the buildings within the district and produce electricity from it to be used within those same buildings.
- District energy systems can make use of a greater variety of emissions-free sources, such as solar thermal, sewer heat, biogas, cold lake water, biomass and ground heat, and combine them at a centralized location to be distributed to the connected buildings. This means DE can take advantage of combining multiple small sources of heating or cooling in ways that single building heating/ cooling systems cannot.
- The efficiency of DE systems often attracts private investment from building owners (in the interest of saving on energy bills) and supports local economic development.
 
Where should it be considered? A minimum intensity of energy use - 140 GJ / sq meter - is generally required for the economics of the steam or water distribution network to be practical. So a moderately-dense to dense set of buildings is optimal. The central plant also takes up a certain amount of space, and if the facility is using geothermal energy, a well field also needs to be drilled. Both of these factors often make it easiest to implement in new, large-scale developments. Many of the first district energy systems in North America were established on university campuses or in hospitals - locations where a large number of buildings were being built all at once and would be managed by one entity. Similarly today, district energy is often easiest to implement in a new, large-scale development. But it can also be retrofit into many situations. 
How would we help a client determine where they could put district energy? 
1. CityInSights energy outputs can be combined with GIS polygons a community's zones to produce a map of energy use by zone for any year that is modelled. Wherever a zone or a small cluster of zones is modelled to require at least 140 MJ / m2, district energy could be feasible. In absence of the GIS data or map representation, we can also look at the spreadsheet of energy use by zone, and find individual zones with 140 GJ+ of energy use in future years.  
2. If there is a whole new community being planned - either greenfield or infill - this is usually an excellent place to consider district energy preferably for at least a somewhat dense urban form. New infill communities give you opportunities to look at using waste heat from existing sewer networks or neighbouring industrial waste heat, which is extra cool. 
3. Large existing or new buildings such as that have large areas of ground that are exposed (e.g. sports fields) or almost exposed (parking lots) are great opportunities to retrofit for geothermal district energy because you can easily add a field of geothermal wells to the area without having to disrupt buildings.
	Any new district energy system we propose should use a renewable or alternative energy source, such as geothermal or ground-source heat exchange, and use of underground waste heat from industry or sewer lines. Building a new district energy system to use natural gas strictly will be more energy-efficient than putting natural gas furnaces or boilers in each building separately, but it is also installing costly infrastructure based on using fossil fuels, which isn't doing our clients any favours. They'll need to spend significantly more in the not-too-distant future to replace the whole thing with a zero emissions alternative. This is one of those cases where whatever we propose should be the right system for when it's still operating 30 years from now.   
What should we do with existing district energy systems? Firstly, make sure you find out whether there are any district energy systems in the community you're working with. City staff don't always know, and if they don't know, you're most likely to find them with a little research, at their universities or hospitals. Unless the system is quite new, existing district energy systems in North America are still generally using natural gas. These can and should be modeled to be more energy-efficient by adding combined heat and power, and they should be switched to zero emissions energy sources. Operationally, the easiest switch for such systems is to go to renewable natural gas. And if you already have a lot of actions to model or your client is new to climate planning, this may be a good enough option to choose. But you should at least be certain to communicate when discussing the actions, and again in the Plan, that the cost of renewable natural gas is forecast to be high, and all forecasts indicate there won't be enough of it to go around so we should preserve it for other purposes. (See the Renewable Natural Gas actions for more details.) If you can't take the time to incorporate district energy into the modelling, your Plan should still include a recommendation 
Where are there district energy systems currently? There are thousands of district energy systems operating in every country in the world, with over 900 district energy systems in North America alone as of 2023. Virtually every major city - including Paris, Vancouver, New York, Boston, Denver, San Francisco, Moscow all have district energy systems. And virtually all of the buildings in Iceland are heated by geothermal district energy. In the UAE and across the Middle East, there's recently been a massive shift to start using district energy for cooling! This will increasingly make sense as the world warms. 
Why isn't it as common in North America as natural gas furnaces? And why is it so common in Europe and especially Scandinavia? In North America, fossil fuel has been so cheap for so long that district energy hasn't become the default way of planning to heat a community. There simply hasn't been much pressure to gain the efficiencies that come with district energy. By contrast, after the oil crisis of the 1970s, many northern European countries passed legislation requiring that any electricity generator also capture and use the waste heat from electricity generation and use it through district energy systems. As a result, there are lots of DE systems in Scandinavia in particular, and also across Europe. With the climate crisis, more North American communities are considering opportunities for DE, but there is much more potential for it to be used as a more comprehensive and default approach to heating an cooling. 

See also: https://www.volts.wtf/p/whats-the-deal-with-district-energy

action_name: Procure zero emissions electricity
Install small, modular nuclear reactors
Install nuclear power generators
description:
A nuclear reactor is a device used to initiate and control a fission nuclear chain reaction or nuclear fusion reactions. Nuclear reactors are used at nuclear power plants for electricity generation. Heat from nuclear fission is passed to a fluid (water or gas), which in turn runs through steam turbines. These turn electrical generators' shafts. Nuclear generated steam can in principle also be used for industrial process heat or for district heating. 

Nuclear reactors do not produce greenhouse gas emissions, and nuclear power plants produce a tremendous amount of energy. A kilogram of uranium-235 (U-235) converted via nuclear processes releases approximately three million times more energy than a kilogram of coal burned conventionally. The power plant operates by controlling and limiting a series of exothermic chain reactions, and harnessing the energy released from those reactions. These exothermic reactions can persist for a long time, and tremendous amounts of water are required to cool the reactors enough to keep them safe. Controlling nuclear reactors is done both manually and using automation. There are automated processes that take over if safety issues are detected. 

Despite automated shut-downs however, extreme seismic events, an extended loss of power, or physical damage from warfare can cause a plant to release radioactivity into the surrounding land, air and water, killing people, plants and animals, causing cancer, and rendering large areas of land and water unusable and uninhabitable. Due to the severity of this risk, nuclear power stations at present are not often built in many parts of the world. in North America, the process to apply for, design, approve and build a new plant is very lengthy. They were popular for a time, and as of 2022, the International Atomic Energy Agency reports there are 422 nuclear power reactors in operation around the world.

action_name: Use heat exchange to heat and cool public infrastructure
description:
Beyond simply using commercial heat pumps, HVAC systems can be designed in many contexts to simply move heat from where it isn’t wanted to where it is. 

For years, organizations as varied as telecom operators and oilsands refineries have used heat exchange systems to transfer excess heat away from equipment or chemical reactions. In some cases this has simply involved purchasing ‘chillers’ that move heat outside and then release it, essentially wasting it. 

In other cases, where the value of the heat is recognized, it has been transferred to places where it’s needed. This avoids the need to burn more fuel (and pay for it) to create more heat. Examples include:
- The Town of Whitby’s Recreation Centre that warms its swimming pool with heat taken from the water used to make the ice rink.

Replace diesel generators with zero-emissions alternatives
description:
Diesel generators are used today in some of the most important, most demanding sectors of the economy: oil & gas drilling, construction, in remote communities, and for data center back-up power. 
However, in addition to diesel being a high-emissions fossil fuel, diesel generators are expensive and inefficient. Energy from diesel generators is 5-10x more expensive than electricity from the grid. Diesel generators are also loud and release harmful air pollutants.
Several zero-emissions options exist for replacing diesel generators.
-  For remote locations that rely on diesel to power much of their heating, cooling and power generation, switching to large grount-mount solar installations with battery storage can very eliminate the need for a significant amount of the diesel generators currently in use. 
- For large-scale electricity back-up in industrial locations, at airports or at large institutions like hospitals, hydrogen-to-power generators are increasingly being used as alternatives to diesel generators. They can sit idle for extended periods without ‘leaking’ energy, and they produce no air pollution when operated. This makes them very valuable for hospitals or seniors residences.

action_name: Switch to green hydrogen fuel

Only green hydrogen is truly zero-emissions, as both blue and grey hydrogen still produce emissions in the upstream portion of natural gas production.

action_name: Use flywheel technology to store and dispatch energy
description: Flywheel systems are kinetic energy storage devices that react instantly when needed. By accelerating a cylindrical rotor (flywheel) to a very high speed and maintaining the energy in the system as rotational energy, flywheel energy storage systems can moderate fluctuations in grid demand. When generated power exceeds load, the flywheel speeds up; when load exceeds generation, the flywheel is slowed to convert the energy for distribution. The plant will provide a response time of less than four seconds to frequency changes. With availability of more than 97%, as demonstrated in earlier small-scale pilots, this technology exceeds the average availability for conventional generators performing frequency regulation. You can install 20 MW / acre. They can be installed in sizes from 100 kW to multi-MW. They last at least 20 years and can dispatch 5000 MWh per unit over their lifetime, making them very low cost / kWh. Their charge and discharge rates are identical.

action_name: Install pumped hydro storage
description:
This refers to a situation in which when you have an excess of energy, you pump water up into a storage area, and when you need energy, you allow the water to flow down from the storage, through turbines to produce electricity. 

In cases in which the same water is cycled through this loop repeatedly, it is referred to a closed loop pumped hydro storage system.

action_name: Store heat underground in sand or in rocks
description:
Underground thermal energy storage (UTES) systems store energy by pumping heat into an underground space (such as a borehole, aquifer or cavern) or a substrate like rock or sand. When it's needed above ground it can be drawn back up using the same pumping system. 	
Sand is a favored thermal energy storage media as it has very high thermal stability allowing it to cycle between ambient air temperature and over 1000°C. The wide temperature range increases energy storage density and system efficiency. Sand is widely available and cheap at about $30 a ton. In an insulated silo it would lose only approximately 	1% of the heat a day.

action_name: Capture excess renewable energy by converting it to hydrogen
description:
When on-site renewable electricity generation systems produce more electricity than can be used on-site at the time, that electricity can be directed back into the grid (if it is connected to the grid), or it may simply be lost. Alternatively, it can be converted into store energy. One way to do this is to send it through electrolysis, which separates water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen can be stored and used as energy at another time.

A Honda facility in Tarronce, California has converted H2 vehicle batteries that can no longer be used in vehicles into a back-up power source for their data center. It replaces a diesel generator, acts as energy storage when excess power is produced from wind or solar, and provides enough ‘instant on’ capacity to react instantly to power outages. It also avoids partially spent batteries from becoming waste.

action_name: Electrify appliances
description: Decarbonizing appliances refers primarily to eliminating appliances that use GHG-emitting energy sources, which are mainly natural gas stoves. However, there are also significant ways to reduce the total power use of electric appliances, reducing overall energy consumption and reducing emissions where electricity is not yet 100% emissions-free. For example, San Francisco incentivizes the purchase of heat pump clothes dryers.

action_name: Install electric resistance space heating
Shift freight transportation from trucks to rail
description:
Moving freight long distances by rail releases far fewer emissions than moving it by truck, even when the locomotives run on diesel fuel. 
While municipalities may not be able to install freight railways within their municipality, when we're working with clients representing larger areas (such as Councils of Govt in the US), we can and should be recommending that their transportation planning include shifting as much long distance freight hauling through their jurisdiction away from trucks to rail. To make this truly effective, they should coordinate this with their neighboring jurisdictions and with freight rail carriers to develop a comprehensive and optimized freight rail network. 
Opportunities within a jurisdiction can be found by looking for locations where there is currently a significant amount of trucking consistently traveling back and forth between suppliers and manufacturers or suppliers and ports. These are routes that could potentially be switched to freight rail links.

action_name: Switch to emissions-free energy for heavy duty transportation
description:
What counts as heavy duty transportation?
Heavy duty transportation (or heavy duty vehicles - HDVs) generally refers to a variety of vehicles ranging from long-distance shipping trucks to construction equipment and vehicles, industrial transportation equipment, and some large-scale port vehicles. The majority of these vehicles fall into Class 7 (weighing 26,000 - 33,000 lbs) and Class 8 (weighing > 33,001 lbs).
Is decarbonizing heavy duty transportation different from other vehicles?
Heavy duty vehicles are different from medium and light duty vehicles in that they carry heavier loads, and in some cases carry them long distances. Both of these qualities mean that these vehicles use a greater amount of energy on an average 'trip' than light or medium duty vehicles do. In the relatively short history of electric vehicles, it has been difficult for a battery to provide enough energy to a HDV for it to complete a reasonable amount of a task or a journey before having to charge again. This is changing as battery capacity increases and vehicle efficiencies improve. Manufacturers have also added hydrogen fuel cells to some HDVs, allowing the hydrogen to act as a secondary source of energy by converting it to electricity when required. This extends the range of these vehicles.

action_name: Switch to emissions-free energy for corporate fleet vehicles
description:
A city or corporate fleet of vehicles is one of the easiest actions to encourage our clients to take, because the return on investment is generally very fast - within 3-5 years. After the initial cost of purchasing the new vehicles and charging/ fueling infrastructure has been paid back, this action will save the corporation significantly every year in fuel and maintenance costs. 

Things to bear in mind:
1. Availability of electric vehicles isn't fast enough yet to meet demand, but many cities (e.g. Halifax, Durham Region in Ontario) are creating coalitions with their utilities and other local fleets and negotiating purchases and better delivery schedules using their combined buying power.
2. ICE vehicles can also be converted to electric vehicles by switching the ICE drive trains to electric drive trains. Ford provides a kit to convert trucks in this way. Doing this reduces waste and energy, and is a great example of circularity - by continuing to use the body and other parts of the vehicle while still achieving the efficiency and emissions reductions coming from electric vehicles.
3. An internal combustion engine is only about 30-45% efficient - meaning only 30% (in small vehicles) to 45% (in larger diesel vehicles) of the energy generated through fuel combustion is actually used to move the vehicle. The rest is wasted. Electric vehicles are over 75% efficient. This fact significantly reduces the draw on the electricity grid that many people are worried about as we switch so much of energy consumption to electricity. 
4. Charging infrastructure comes in more forms all the time - from Level 1 - 3 chargers, to in-ground, wireless chargers, to pantograph chargers for buses. We do sometimes estimate roughly how many chargers our clients will need, but we generally recommend they develop a Fleet Electrification Plan that will ensure their charging infrastructure is optimized to the specific needs of their fleet.

action_name: Switch to emissions-free energy for personal use vehicles
description:
Decarbonized vehicles are generally defined as those that produce zero emissions when being operated. This includes electric vehicles, where the electricity that powers them is produced from zero emissions sources such as solar, windor hydro power. It also includes hydrogen fuel cell vehicles, where the hydrogen is produced without generating emissions (i.e. green hydrogen). 

Compressed natural gas and liquid natural gas are not zero emissions fuels, and vehicles that run on these fuels are not decarbonized vehicles.

An internal combustion engine is only about 30-45% efficient - meaning only 30% (in small vehicles) to 45% (in larger diesel vehicles) of the energy generated through fuel combustion is actually used to move the vehicle. The rest is wasted. Electric vehicles are over 75% efficient. This fact significantly reduces the draw on the electricity grid that many people are worried about as we switch so much of energy consumption to electricity. 
4. Charging infrastructure comes in more forms all the time - from Level 1 - 3 chargers, to in-ground, wireless chargers, to pantograph chargers for buses. We do sometimes estimate roughly how many chargers our clients will need, but we generally recommend they develop a Fleet Electrification Plan that will ensure their charging infrastructure is optimized to the specific needs of their fleet.

action_name: Replace the use of petroleum-based diesel fuel with biodiesel or renewable diesel.
description:
Biodiesels are fuels that are chemically similar to petroleum diesel. In many cases, you can use 100% biodiesel in a diesel engine without needing to modify the engine. In that case, biodiesel can produce about 78% less emissions when burned than petroleum diesel.  What’s different about biodiesel is that it’s made from soybeans, corn, or food fats rather than refined from fossil fuels. It's considered ‘renewable’ because of that fact - it comes from a source that can be replenished within a person’s lifetime. The thinking there is that the natural carbon cycle of the planet incorporates a certain amount of CO2 in the atmosphere being taken up by plants (soybeans or whatever) and then being released again back into the atmosphere. Climate change has occurred because we started digging up coal and such, and releasing way more CO2 than can be accommodated within the natural cycle of plant growth and death. So if you can get fuels from that natural plant cycle rather than from fossil fuels, you are working within the limits of that natural cycle, and the fuel can be considered ‘carbon neutral’. That all makes sense except for a few things:
1. Most importantly, even if we replaced 100% of existing diesel use with biodiesel, we’d still be burning it at a much faster rate than it can be absorbed by the natural carbon cycle. We basically can’t grow the soybeans fast enough to compensate for all the biodiesel we’d be burning. So in that sense, the fuel is not carbon neutral.
2. Biodiesel tends to get more viscous when it’s cold, so it’s often blended (20% biodiesel to 80% petroleum diesel is relatively common) to avoid that problem. Depending on how it’s produced, it can also be expensive, which is another reason to blend it with fossil fuels. And as soon as you use a blend, you’re back to releasing much more emissions.
3. It does still produce many of the other air pollutants that petroleum diesel produces - in some cases less than petroleum diesel and in some cases more. 
4. Producing biodiesel generally requires a lot of water - more than petroleum diesel production. 
5. Depending on how and where it is produced, the full lifecycle of creating biodiesel can generate more emissions particularly from the electricity required in the production and from the transportation of the fuel - although both of those have emissions-free alternatives. So these issues can be resolved. 
6. And finally, producing enough soybeans and corn for fuel requires that valuable arable land is taken away from food production. At the scale at which these plants are required to produce biodiesel, this starts to impact our ability to produce enough crops to eat.

action_name: Eliminate emissions from ports
description:
The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach are world leaders in decarbonizing  their ports both by requiring docked shios to use shore power and by converting all of their port cranes, vehicles and equipment to electric models. They have also extended (electric) rail links closer to freight offloading sites to increase efficiency. 
Shore Power
For a municipality, one of the most basic ways to support marine decarbonization is to provide and require the use of shore power by all ships while docked. Not only does this stop ships from burning fossil fuels, it also reduces air pollution in the area around the port. 
Considerations
- In major ports, it is important that enough power and plug infrastructure is provided to allow all docked ships to connect, and to ensure that ships can load and unload freight and passengers in the same docked position in which they can access power. 
- It is also important to work with utilities and port authorities to ensure that the demand for power from these ships can be accommodated by the grid and by on-site renewable energy generation.
- At present (2025) not all container ships or cruise ships have the ability to connect to shore power, but as ports add the requirement to stop using polluting fuels while in port, this is changing. 
- From the munipality’s perspective, making it mandatory to use shore power (initially only if a ship has the required connectors, but ultimately requring this for all ships) ensures emissions are reduced and also helps justifies the investment in charging infrastructure. 
Where is this occurring?
The State of California has made it mandatory for all ships to plug into power while docked, if they are able to do so.

In Canada, in 2025, 4 of 17 municipal port authorities had at least some shore power for cruise ships and container ships: Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Montreal and Halifax. Proposed expansions to Victoria’s, Montreal’s and Churchill’s ports are expected to include additions of shore power. (Source: https://oceansnorth.org/2025/09/15/new-analysis-benchmarks-progress-on-shore-power-implimentation-at-canadian-ports/)

China requires that all ships connect to shore power while docked if they are able to do so. The port of Shanghai has power connections for virtually docking locations. 

The EU requires ships to plug into shore power at all major ports starting in 2030, and requires all ports to provide shore power by 2035. The port of Hamburg currently provides power to virtually all dock sites in its port.

action_name: Decarbonize off-road vehicles
description: Off-road vehicles includes everything from personal all-terrain vehicles to large construction equipment, mining equipment, etc. The mining industry was one of the earliest adopters of electric heavy duty equipment, which it did to eliminate poisonous fumes from underground operations. These vehilces are more commonly used than most of our clients realize.

action_name: Switch to zero-emissions engines for rail
Eliminate emissions from aviation
description:
How much of a problem is it?
Aviation accounts for 3% of global emissions annually, and according to then IEA will account for 3.5% by 2030. 
There are two main ways in which aviation contributes to global warming. (See RMI report link below for source.)  
1. The aviation industry contributes approximately 2.4% of global CO2 emissions from aviation fuel, which is primarily kerosene.
2. The warming impact of contrails (or contrail cirrus) is estimated to contribute an additional 61% of that aviation fuel impact by reflecting  back heat that would otherwise escape into the atmosphere. 

This is a challenging sector
This is a sector which is proving difficult to decarbonize.  Here are some of the main reasons:
1. High energy density fuel: Flight requires fuels with high energy density, and we don’t have many alternatives for those kinds of fuels. (See the SAF action for details.) 
2. Electric planes: Electric planes are also in operation, but they are small planes that can only fly distances up to 1,200 km. Until a truly decarbonized solution is realized on a commercial scale (which isn’t expected on a large scale until the 2050 timeframe) the best way we have to reduce emissions from flying is by flying less. (See the Electric planes action for details.)
3. Improvements in energy efficiency are smaller than increases in flights: Before the pandemic, the efficiency of jet engines was improving by about 3% annually; however, the number of flights taken was increasing by 5% annually.
4. Contrails and N2O emissions: Non-CO2 emissions from planes at high altitudes contribute up to three times the warming effect of CO2 emissions. This includes contrails and N2O emissions. Some actions, like reducing nighttime flights, could improve this. But a comprehensive solution is not expected in the near term.Work to reduce contrails is underway by the Contrail Impact Task Force, which is led by the Rocky Mountain Institute and includes American Airlines, Boeing and the Imperial College London among others. 
5. Offsets: If effective offsets exist, they are seen by some as a valid way to reduce emissions until these other options are able to completely eliminate the global warming impact of flight. 

When do we include it in our plans? 
Emissions from aviation should be included in the climate action plans of any area that has an airport within its boundwry, or that is used by the populatioj residing within its boundary . This requires some judgement - obviously we don’t need to account for flights taken from every single airport any resident of the community flies from in a given year. But if there is an airport commonly used by municipal residents, for example, we should make efforts to include its emissions in our baseline, and include reduction actions. In addition, there are rules regarding howthe portion of an airport’s emissions that a community is responsible for, that should be followed . See the GPC protocol for details. 
How can we reduce emissions from aviation?

1. Switch to sustainable aviatIon fuel. (See the Sustainable Aviation Fuel child action for details.
2. Switching to electric planes. Electric planes currently have a limited range, but some industry experts are confident that this limitation will be overcome in the relatively near future. 
3. Offset emissions with local, proven offsets.
4. Fly less.

Note that presently there is no mitigation action for contrails, but it is being worked on.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel
See the ‘child action’ for details. Alternative fuels with lower emissions are called ‘sustainable aviation fuel’ or SAF. 
Electric planes
Electric short-haul planes are already in use in locations such as Victoria, B.C. Presently they can generally fly up to 1,200 km with a small number of passengers.
What reductions has the international aviation industry committed to?
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) participates in COPs and overseas the industry’s commitments to international emissions reduction initiatives. The aviation industry as a whole has committed to a 50% reduction in emissions relative to 2005 by 2050. However, individual airlines have made their own commitments:
- United, Airlines, 
- Virgin Atlantic,
- KLM, 
- British Airways, and 
- Lufthansa have all made various commitments to reducing their emissions.

Airports have also made commitments to provide SAF, and to eliminating emissions from their own operations. Oslo airport began offering SAF in 2016, and LAX followed shortly thereafter.

action_name: Reduce driving ICE vehicles - both the number of trips and the distances driven
description:
Why is this important? 
Reducing people's dependence on ICE vehicles is part of an overall need to eliminate fossil fuel combustion for transportation. Simplistically, we may think all we need to do is simply switch all our existing vehicles to decarbonized models. However there are a few problems with this: 
- EVs are still significantly more expensive than ICE vehicles, although most types and models are expected to be priced at parity with ICEs by 2030-2032.
- There aren't enough EVs being produced fast enough to swap them all out, so logistically this is impossible.
- A complete charging and fueling infrastructure network isn't in place yet, although it's growing rapidly in most places.
- Less significantly, EVs are significantly heavier than ICE vehicles, so if we swapped out ICEs one-for-one with EVs, roadways would have more wear and could experience particular problems during heat waves, ferries could carry fewer vehicles, etc.

Are there other benefits from doing this? 
There are also lots of good reasons to drive less, and to transport goods less:
- It reduces congestion within cities. With cities expected to continue growing, this will become even more important in coming years.
- Emissions from ICE vehicles are a significant source of air pollution which in turn causes or exacerbates asthma and other lung diseases.
- Vehicle maintenance and fuel is consistently the first or second largest average household expense in North America. If we can stop building communities in such a way that residents are required to rely on owning a personal vehicle, we can make life much more affordable, especially for lower income people.
- Active transportation (i.e. biking, walking, using scooters, etc.) significantly improves peoples' physical and mental health, reduces sick days taken, is consistently reported to be a more enjoyable commute, and reduces health costs associated with diseases caused by inactivity.  (See the Increase active transportation mode share action for more details.) 
- Car sharing is a step in the right direction, as you get more people traveling with less emissions. This is a relatively minor impact on emissions, but it can be a useful interim objective to increase car sharing.
- Taking transit significantly reduces emissions even taking into consideration the fact that the vehicles are larger. (See the Transit actions for more details.)
- Reducing the number of ICE vehicles on the roads also decreases noise which has been shown to be an issue for bird populations. As traffic noise levels increase, bird populations tend to decrease because the birds are less able to hear each other and so less able to communicate with mating partners or flocks.
- Active transportation is very inexpensive both for the traveler and for the city or region from an infrastructure perspective. From a city's perspective, 1 km of active transportation infrastructure is much less costly to build in terms of materials, labor and land use. It is also much less costly to maintain even in northern climates.  
- Purchasing goods made or grown locally, rather than shipping them in reduces freight emissions, energy use, etc. required in that transportation, reduces costs associated with transportation, stimulates the local economy, and makes the community more resilient/ independent.  

For all of these reasons and more, taking actions to reduce the number of ICE vehicle trips within all communities is important, relatively inexpensive, and an extremely beneficial step in decarbonization.	 

If it's so obvious, why isn't everyone already doing this? 
Generally the biggest challenge in North America to achieve a meaningful reduction in ICE vehicle use is changing people's habits and the car culture in which we live. Car ownership has become entrenched in everything from our city planning to how we mark children's coming-of-age to status symbols.  Those communities that have successfully begun to reduce car use have: 
1. Taken a multi-pronged approach to  the problem - offering both carrots (e.g. paying people per km taking transit, biking or walking) and sticks (charging for ICE vehicle parking, and reducing parking) to change behaviors. 
2. Taken a very flexible and dynamic approach to designing new active transportation routes such that when one proposed route causes a problem it's adjusted within hours or days.
3. Diligently tracked indicators of success or failure, including counting riders on transit at a detailed level, counting cyclists and pedestrians, tracking revenue for businesses along active transportation routes, etc. 

How do we measure whether and how much this is changing? 
There are a few ways to measure this change:
- Vehicle kilometres / miles travelled - also known as VKT or VMT - are a measure of the total distance travelled by all vehicles within a city over the course of a year. Many cities and regions have calculations of these numbers, and their transportation departments use traffic counters and modelling to monitor how this changes over time.
- Vehicle registrations - the number and type of vehicles registered in a community can be reviewed annually to identify trends in vehicle purchasing and ownership.
- Transit ridership, bike and pedestrian counters can provide real-time and highly location-specific data useful when expanding and improving these modes of transportation.

How do we do it? 
The sub-actions for this action describe many of the ways in which this can be done. There are also a variety of case studies associated with this action and/ or its sub-actions that provide good examples of where it has been done.

action_name: Work/ study from home
description: Working or studying from home reduces the need to travel to and from work or school, and eliminates the emissions associated with those trips.

action_name: Decrease vehicle km traveled
Reduce high-emissions travel
description: Reduce community-wide travel through any mode of transportation that generates high amounts of greenhouse gases.

action_name: Reduce emission-generating business travel
description: This includes reducing all types of trips that produce emissions, from reducing flights to conferences and meetings, to walking or biking to another office for a local meeting.

action_name: Decrease fuel use by improving vehicle and driver behaviours
description: If this is being used with ICE vehicles, the value is relatively small, and it should only be a temporary measure. In EVs, it's a valid way to reduce energy use.

action_name: Improve efficiency of marine transportation
description: This should be a temporary measure with decarbonization of marine transportation as the ultimate action.

action_name: Improve fuel efficiency in vehicles or use 'cleaner' fuels
description: This is not a recommended action because the need to get to zero emissions vehicles is now so urgent that the lifespan of (even more fuel efficient) ICE vehicles will cause us to still be generating emissions too late.

action_name: Switch to electric planes for short flights
description:
As of 2024, commercial electric planes are able to fly up to 1200 km. These planes are small, taking a maximum of approximately 20 passengers. 

While the industry continues to work on expanding their range, and increasing the size of plane, manufacturers are also developing planes to carry freight only that are operated remotely.

action_name: Switch to wind-powered cargo ships
description:
A 100% wind-powered cargo ship that can dramatically cut transatlantic shipping times and carbon emissions, according to its operator, could launch in early 2027.
The vessel can hold approximately five times the capacity of a cargo plane, says the company. Vela positions its services somewhere between conventional sea and air freight: quicker than sea freight, slower than air freight, and with much lower emissions than either.
The trimaran, with two smaller hulls on either side of a central hull, will be propelled by sails extending 200 feet (61 meters) above the waterline, with onboard power for living and working quarters, plus temperature-controlled cargo holds, provided by solar panels and two hydro generators. Vela says it will travel at an average speed of 14 knots — equivalent to the speed of a modern container ship — between New Jersey and Normandy or Bordeaux, France.
French company Vela will run a service between France and the US with its custom-made seacraft. The 220-foot (67-meter) long, 82-foot (25-meter) wide vessel will be able to transport just over 400 metric tons of cargo, and was designed with the input of Vela cofounder François Gabart, a professional yacht racer and the fastest sailor to circumnavigate the globe solo.
A life cycle assessment, conducted by Vela and climate consultancy group Carbone 4, calculated carbon emissions from the North Atlantic crossing would be up to 96% less than a conventional container ship, and up to 99% less than air freight.
With everything factored in, Vela says it can load, cross the Atlantic and unload in 15 days.

action_name: Decrease aviation emissions by using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
description:
Switching to Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is the primary way the industry is currently working to reduce emissions from aviation. SAF is basically renewable natural gas for planes. It still produces emissions, but it is derived from renewable sources rather than fossil fuels. It is often a blend of traditional jet fuel and up to 50% biofuels, which may be made from everything from soybeans to canola oil. Biofuel can be added directly to existing fuel tanks and does not require modifications to engines to be used. It is increasingly being used, especially for long-haul flights. 
Why is it considered to be ‘zero emissions’?
This fuel is officially considered to produce zero emissions because it is produced from plants which absorbed the same amount of emissions as they grew that they will release when they are burned as fuel. However this is only true if the plants and waste used to create it are replenished at the same rate it's used, which isn't the case. If we switched all flights to SAF immediately, we'd be emitting much faster than plants would be growing to sequester those emissions. 
Limited availability
The renewable sources from which SAF can be made are limited, so it is currently difficult to produce in sufficient quantities. In 2018, 15 million liters of biofuel used for aviation still only accounted for 0.1% of the total aviation fuel used.Some estimate that it is can only be ramped up to a maximum of 2% of all aviation fuel, but The IEA anticipates biofuel will make up 10% of all aviation fuel by 2030 and 20% by 2040. 
We also need to ensure that we are not diverting crops relied upon for food. The solution is believed to lie in using more  food and organic waste to produce biofuel. 
Expensive
Partially because of its limited availability, SAF is much more expensive than jet fuel. And jet fuel is already airlines’s greatest cost. This makes switching to it difficult withou significantly increasing costs to passengers.

action_name: Switch to emissions-free energy for ferries
description: The vast majority of ferries run on fossil fuels such as diesel. Current industry trends suggest transitioning to electric ferries powered with zero-emissions electricity is the best zero-emissions alternative. See the San Francisco case study.

action_name: Reduce generation of waste
Decrease waste sent to an emitting landfill
Improve waste treatment
Implement systems to produce 'renewable' versions of natural gas
Add low-impact development facilities (LID) or green stormwater infrastructure to reduce the amount of water being processed in the sewer or stormwater system.
description:
Green stormwater infrastructure, or Low Impact Development (LID) facilities slow stormwater and reduce the total volume of it that enters the stormwater system, or the sewer system in the case they're combined. In combined stormwater/ sewer systems, reducing the amount of stormwater being processed will reduce the amount of energy required to treat it, and this in turn reduces the emissions generated to produce that energy. 
LID incorporates plants, engineered soils, and natural processes to capture stormwater runoff close to its source. Stormwater enters the LID and flows into the engineered soil layer with the ability to capture and filter stormwater. Specially selected plants then absorb the water or it evaporates. Any excess water that isn't used by the plants and soils drains into the stormwater system.

action_name: Separate stormwater capture from wastewater system
Build small-scale reservoirs on agricultural land to reduce irrigation
Reduce conventional tillage practices for crops
description:
Reducing or eliminating tillage of crops reduces emissions in several ways: 
1. It reduces the need to drive agricultural vehicles, reducing the emissions from those vehicles. 
2. Not tilling and not driving over soil reduces compaction of the soil, which in turn supports better crop growth and carbon sequestration.

The specific calculation used for the CMCOG project was as follows: 
Number of acres converted from intensive tillage to non-tilled saves 0.77 tonne CO2e/year/acre. (Source: Journal of Advances in Agronomy and Crop Science. See References below.)

action_name: Implement diversified crop rotation on some or all crop lands
description:
Emissions calculations by crop can be found here: https://apps.carboncloud.com/climatehub/agricultural-reports/benchmarks/c47770c9-701d-470f-9919-de4dadf9e8b6

Crop Diversification & Changes in Crop Sequencing (Source: https://apps.msuextension.org/montguide/guide.html?sku=MT201704AG )
- Pulse crops enable producers to diversify their production and cope with increasing variability in temperature and precipitation
- Pulse crops have substantial rotational benefits for wheat and barley production including improved soil fertility, increased water use efficiency, and disruption of pest and disease cycles
- By replacing summer fallow with pulse crops, farmers are able to increase cropping intensity while improving soil health and potentially increasing soil moisture retention
- Chickpeas, dry peas and lentils consume less water than spring wheat, making them well-adapted to increasingly hotter summer temperatures

Capturing Carbon in the Soil (Source: https://apps.msuextension.org/montguide/guide.html?sku=MT201704AG )
- If moisture is available, the inclusion of cover crops as temporary vegetative cover between agricultural crops can add carbon to soil and may also capture excess plant-available nitrogen that was not used by the previous crop in the rotation, reducing the release of nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas.

action_name: Increase use of precision agriculture technologies in farming.
description:
"Precision agriculture technologies" include a growing number of sophisticated agricultural tools that reduce everything from the amount of pesticide and herbicide applied to fuel used to irrigation. Some examples include: 
- Controlled Traffic Farming, which reduces fuel use in farm vehicles;
- Variable nutrient application rates, which reduces N2O emissions from excess fertilizer application; and, 
- Variable irrigation rates, which reduces emissions from energy used to run irrigation systems.

action_name: Improve efficiency of agricultural irrigation
description: Optimizing agricultural irrigation efficiency requires that as little water as possible is wasted (through leakage or evaporation for example), that irrigation doesn't draw from water treated to a drinking water standard, and that moving water is done using highly energy-efficient systems, preferably powered by renewable sources.

action_name: Increase use of rotational grazing
description: [To be completed]

action_name: Install anaerobic digesters on individual farms
description: See 'Implement anaerobic digesters...' action for more details on anaerobic digestion generally.

action_name: Substituting and adjusting livestock feed
description: Most of the emissions from animal production come from methane released through the digestive process of livestock, and from manure management. Substituting and adjusting livestock feed can reduce these emissions–for example, by moving from corn to barley, adding seaweed or other food additives, or switching to high-quality forages like alfalfa.

action_name: Improve energy efficiency in agricultural operations and rural businesses
description: Improving energy efficiency in agricultural operations begins with an energy audit that is appropriate to the type of agricultural operation. Based on this evaluation, recommendations can be made regarding everything from locations of equipment and tasks, to improving building insulation, to adding and switching technologies.

action_name: Use gravity-based water distribution
Improve water treatment and distribution efficiency
description:
Water (and wastewater) treatment are often the single largest consumers of energy within the portfolio of a city’s corporately owned facilities. At the same time, they are often older than other more public-facing which means they use older, less efficient technologies and approaches than are now available. 

Water treatment technologies that should be considered for upgrades include pumps both within treatment faciliities and throughout the distribution network: 
- Motors for fans and pumps can be replaced with variable speed models that automatically adjust the intensity with which they operate (and so also the power consumed) based on what’s required. 
- Water distribution can reduce the need for pumps if it can take advantage of gravity. Treatment facilities and water storage that is located above the water’s destinations can simply flow down rather than requiring pumping.

The specific changes required will vary by facility and require detailed, engineering-level analyses. For SSG’s community modelling, we can generally use simple expressions of improvements such as, “Overall efficiency of water treatment is improved by 5% by 2035.” If we are developing a plan for a water utility, we will want to be more specific and work with staff to identify where the best opportunities exist for improvements.

action_name: Decrease water volumes delivered through plumbing fixtures to meet rather than exceed requirements
Decrease use of treated fresh water through changes in behaviour and processes
description:
Baseline Water Consumption
According to World Health Organization, between 50 and 100 litres of clean water are required per person per day to ensure that basic needs are met and few health problems arise. 
By contrast: 
- In Canada in 2023, residential water use per person was 223 litres, up 8% from the previous year. Total per capita water use - including residential, industrial, commercial and other water use - in 2019 was 411 litres. 
- In the U.S. average per capita water consumption in 2024 was 310 litres (82 gallons) / day according to the EPA. 
- In Chile, average per capita water use is 196 litres daily. 
- The global average per capita daily water consumption is 157 litres daily.
Energy Consumption, Costs and Emissions
The treatment and pumping of fresh water to residents of cities and towns require large amounts of electricity, and this constitutes significant ongoing operational cost for municipalities or counties. Emissions from water treatment come from the generation of electricity consumed to pump and treat the water. So reducing these emissions requires switching to zero-emissions electricity generation. It also requires reducing the total energy consumption, to ensure there is enough electricity available to meet all our needs especially as we electrify transportation, building heating, etc.
Current Approach
For years, fresh water has been viewed as a virtually limitless commodity. As a result, our water distribution systems encourage us to use highly-treated water that meets ‘drinking quality’ standards for virtually any use. A single source provides water to our taps for drinking, to our toilets, to our garden hoses, to our fire hydrants and car washes, and to our industrial cooling towers. All of this water is treated to a drinking level standard even though just over half of it is used for drinking (based on the Canadian figures provided above). This means that almost half of this water is over-treated relative to the purposes for which it will be used. This in turn means we are using more energy and incurring more costs than we need to. 
This is further complicated by changing infrastructure quality and efficiency:
- Urban water distribution networks have been built up over time, and most of these systems experience leakage to varying extents. Because this infrastructure is difficult to access (and often in the worst condition in the oldest parts of a city, where it is also generally most difficult to access), this leakage can result in significant losses of treated water. For example, Halifax Water, in the capital of Nova Scotia, Canada, estimates that it loses approximately 40% of all of the water it treats to leaks. 
- Pumps have become much more efficient since many water treatment utilities were constructed in urban centres in North and South America. However, most water treatment facilities still use at least some old, inefficient pumps, dramatically increasing their total energy consumption and costs.

In addition, growing populations in urban communities are increasing the need for water, further increasing demand from treatment facilities that were designed to meet much smaller needs. Providers that continue to use the traditional approaches to water treatment and distribution find themselves constantly having to plan for expansion while also maintaining their existing, expensive and inefficient facilities.
Solutions
Fortunately there are many ways in which energy consumption and resulting emissions generation can be reduced in water treatment facilities. Here are some of the key ones (more details are provided in thenassociated child actions):
1. Demand-side management (DSM), from tap aerators to low flow toilets;
2. Replacing pumps with new, more efficient models;
3. Adding renewable energy generation such as solar panels and wind turbines to water treatment facilities to reduce emissions from the power consumed at the site;
4. Adding hydro generators and battery storage to distribution network, particular in areas where gravity moves the water through the piping;
5. Using heat exchange within a facility, through geothermal piping, with neighbouring buildings, and even with sewer pipes to keep water from freezing in cold seasons and climates;
6. Limiting the uses of fully treated water and providing lower qualities of water to (for example) golf courses for irrigation and car washes;
7. Requiring the use of rainwater for watering residential landscaping, encouraging landscaping that requires little water, and discouraging the planting of lawns;
8. Detecting and repairing leaks throughout the distribution network.

action_name: Repair leaks in water distribution networks to reduce loss of treated water
Use grey water, rainwater, or untreated water wherever possible
Increase fresh water storage
Recycle grey and black (i.e. wastewater or sewage) into drinking water
description:
Wastewater from our sewers can be treated sufficiently to return it to a drinking water quality. This is increasingly being done in areas like California and Israel, where droughts are persisting or water shortages are becoming critical as populations grow. Doing so reduces the amount of fresh water drawn from natural sources, prolonging global water availability, while also providing opportunities for heat to be extracted from wastewater, and for the 'sludge' to be used as fuel for heating, industrial uses, or electricity generation.

In many locations, wastewater that has been treated to a reusable standard (whether it's to a drinking water level or lower) is transported in purple pipes that can be seen for example, above ground, providing water to golf courses. As a result, this action is often referred to as 'purple pipes'.

action_name: Re-introduce animal species such as beavers, that protect and increase natural water sources.
Plant trees beside rivers
description:
Planting trees increases carbon sequestration within the trees; however this action focuses specifically on planting trees beside rivers, as a way to protect sources of freshwater. This action is beneficial even if the river itself is not directly drawn from for water consumption. The trees:
- increase shade over the river, decreasing evaporation of fresh water;
- create large root systems below the river which slow water flow, turbidity and river bed erosion during storm events. 

This also provides better habitat for river-dwelling and riparian animals, contributing to increased biodiversity.

action_name: Increase vegetation (native, resilient trees and plants), and maintain them using practices that increase carbon sequestered in soils and vegetation
description:
Action Description
This action refers to planting trees or other types of vegetation to increase the total amount of carbon being drawn out of the air and incorporated into plant growth. 
Background
Natural carbon sequestration is another name for the basic process plants use to grow. Trees, shrubs and grasses all take gaseous carbon from the air and transform it into the solid form of more tree, more shrub and more grass.  However quantifying natural sequestration is complicated. The amount of carbon sequestered depends on the following (and many other considerations):
- The species of tree or plant, 
- The suitability of the tree or plant for the plant hardiness zone in which they're planted,
- The amount of sunlight and moisture level the tree or plant receives in the specific location in which they're planted,
- The presence of pests and diseases that will make the tree or plant less healthy, and
- Maintenance of healthy living conditions over time.
The amount of carbon sequestered varies significantly based on where you are on the planet. In general, trees that grow in humid climates nearer to the equator will sequester much more carbon over their lifetimes than trees that are native to regions further from the equator. 
Implications for the actions we model
This has implications that we see in our modelling. For example, in the baseline year of our climate action plan for the Central Midlands Council of Govts in South Carolina, we discovered that in 2022, vegetation sequestered 32% of their total (Basic+) emissions. That's 4.2 Megatonnes of CO2e sequestered annually, which is much more than what we would see in the same sized area anywhere in Canada. And that's because of the types of trees growing in SC, the length of their growing season, the absence of a harsh winter, etc.        
As a result, we realized that in regions like South Carolina, we can lean more on tree planting, and restoration of former forests in our climate action plans, than we would in many other climates. So we modelled two ambitious actions for CMCOG, one for tree planting and one for forest restoration, and we also constrained the expansion of community boundaries throughout the region. These actions together will eliminate over 35 Megatonnes of CO2e between 2025 and 2050, in this region. The same number of trees planted in Canada would achieve a much smaller reduction.  

In general....
In most of the communities we work with, in less tropical regions of the Americas, tree planting can achieve only a small fraction of what occurs in South Carolina. So although many people would love to think we can plant our way out of the climate crisis, that is not possible. However, in these other regions, tree planting should still be included in order to reduce emissions and energy consumption, but also with a significant emphasis on improving tree cover to reduce outdoor heat, improving and restoring biodiversity, reducing air pollution, and absorbing and diverting stormwater.
What about tree planting as a way of offsetting our emissions?
Important details:
1. The concept of ‘additionality’ is fundamental to the credibility of this action, and means that in order for planting trees to count as a climate action (whether to reduce a community’s own emissions or to sell as carbon credits or offsets), the trees included must be ‘in addition’ to what would been present in a ‘business-as-usual’ situation. For example, a reduction in emissions can be claimed for planting trees that would not otherwise have been planted. A reduction can also be claimed for trees are allowed to continue growing that would otherwise have been logged.  However, a reduction cannot be claimed, nor can carbon credits be sold for not harvesting trees that wouldn’t or couldn’t have been harvested anyways because for example, they were on steep slopes or along the edges of highways where logging would be unsightly. 
2. In order for trees to absorb the emissions claimed in emissions inventories or sold as carbon credits, they must survive and be kept healthy for years. This means the trees chosen must be: 
- Hardy in the zone in which they are being planted, 
- Tolerant of the moisture or dryness they will experience in the location, 
- Reasonably resistant to pests, fungi and diseases they may be attacked by in the location,
- Tolerant of urban pollution if planted in an urban setting, 
- Kept healthy, watered and undamaged while establishing roots, and growing.
Related Assumptions:
- Each tree must have a minimum canopy value of 236 sq. ft, which is at least a 20 ft canopy at maturity. Source: https://www.snwa.com/rebates/wsl/terms-tree-enhancement.html

action_name: Purchase offsets for emissions that cannot currently be eliminated
description:
Purchasing offsets should only be considered appropriate for consideration for local residual emissions - that is, emissions for which the entity is responsible but that cannot currently be eliminated. Some believe that not being able to afford to eliminate them is a valid reason to purchase offsets. Others find innovative ways to fund the unaffordable. This is where judgement comes in. Always advise a client that this is the international 'best practice' - to only use these for emissions that cannot be eliminated, to continually look for ways to eliminate the residuals, and then to stop using offsets as soon as a way to eliminate them is found. 

When purchased, offsets should be purchased from credible source such as goldstandard.org or offset.climateneutralnow.org. 

Another alternative is to develop an internal offset program that reinvests locally to reduce emissions.

action_name: Reduce IPPU emissions from cement manufacturing by accepting 'weaker' strengths of concrete where appropriate.
description:
Industrial product and process use emissions are those that are generated not as a result of the type of energy being used, but because of another chemical reaction or a product being used within the manufacturing process. 
- Changing our cement strength standards to use cements that are strong enough for each particular job, rather than requiring a single, very strong concrete for all jobs. (Currently in N. America, we often require just a single standard of strength for all jobs. However,  in reality, a concrete sidewalk does not require as much strength as a supporting structure in a high-rise building.) Manufacturing lower strengths of cement in particular ways, can produce less emissions per unit of cement manufactured. Cities can encourage a greater variety of cement strengths by building these standards into their municipal and community building standards.

action_name: Reduce IPPU emissions from cement manufacturing
description:
Industrial product and process use emissions are those that are generated not as a result of the type of energy being used, but because of another chemical reaction or a product being used within the manufacturing process. 
Cement Manufacturing: 
Traditional cement manufacturing involves converting limestone to lime, which is the primary reactive ingredient in cement clinker. This conversion releases CO2 as a byproduct. In fact, up to 2/3 of all emissions from cement manufacturing come from this chemical reaction. (The remaining third comes from burning fossil fuels to achieve temperatures of up to 1,500 degrees Celsius to cause this reaction to occur. These are the energy portion of cement manufacturing's emissions, which are dealt with in another action.) 
The main alternatives to decarbonizing the IPPU emissions from the cement industry presently (2026) are: 
- Changing our cement strength standards to use cements that are strong enough for each particular job, rather than requiring a single, very strong concrete for all jobs. (Currently in N. America, we often require just a single standard of strength for all jobs. However, in reality, a concrete sidewalk does not require as much strength as a supporting structure in a high-rise building.) Manufacturing lower strengths of cement in particular ways, can produce less emissions per unit of cement manufactured. Cities can encourage a greater variety of cement strengths by building these standards into their municipal and community building standards.
- To replace the clinker used in cement by using supplementary cementitious materials, such as calcine clay. 
- Carbon capture and utilization or storage may be appropriate for cement kiln process emissions.
