description: Passing regulations simply requiring oil refineries to reduce their emissions by a certain percentage annually, and leaving it up to them to determine how has been successful in a number of communities.	We have modelled this for Regina, Saskatchewan.

action_name: Use grey water or recycled water rather than fresh water for industrial cooling
description: A significant amount of energy is require to treat water to a drinking water standard even though this water ends up being used for purposes that would be as well served by a lower quality of water requiring less treatment. Increasingly, industrial facilities with cooling towers or equipment that requires cooling, are using wastewater for this purpose. Alberta oil sands operators have been doing this for decades.

action_name: Decarbonize the energy used in concrete and steel manufacturing
description:
A number of technologies are being used and more are in the pre-commercial stages of development for concrete and steel manufacturing. These include:
1. Using electric arc furnaces to produce steel.
2. Using hydrogen for processes requiring high temperatures.
3. Using electricity in processes that produce different chemical reactions  than traditional steel manufacturing.
4. Batteries are being developed that can produce 1,500 - 1,800 degree Celsius heat. (Antora Energy, Rondo Energy)

action_name: Reduce IPPU emissions from steel production
description:
Proportion of global emissions:
Steel manufacturing globally makes up 7-10% of emissions. (https://www.marketplace.org/2022/03/21/the-eu-has-sworn-off-russian-steel-that-could-be-bad-news-for-the-environment/) 

Sources
The traditional approach to producing steel produces emissions from two major sources:
Source 1. 
The chemical reaction between coal and iron oxide, which produces iron and CO2. This action addresses this first source of emissions. 
Source 2. 
The combustion of fossil fuels to generate high enough temperatures for the necessary chemical reactions and to make the steel pliable so it can be rolled, cast or molded. This second source is addressed by actions related to decarbonizing the energy used in industrial processes, which is discussed in other actions. Note however, that electricity is not generally believed to be able to get a furnace hot enough to catalyze this reaction. Green hydrogen and renewable natural gas can be burned to provide the temperatures required. Generally we consider steel-making a good use of green hydrogen, because there are no well-established/ proven-at-scale alternative solutions at this time (2024).  We also sometimes advocate for renewable natural gas to be used for this purpose, at least as a temporary measure until a better solution is found.
Addressing the first source of emissions: 
Background: 
Steel is more than 95% iron, and the rest is carbon. In nature, iron generally exists as iron oxide. To purify it into high quality steel, the bond between the iron and oxygen needs to be broken and the oxygen needs to bond with something else. This is traditionally done by adding coal (carbon) into a furnace with the iron ore and heating both to a very high temperature at which the oxygen - iron bond breaks, much purer iron is left and the oxygen bonds with carbon instead and to produce carbon dioxide. This type of steel production therefore produces CO2 firstly from this chemical reaction. It also produces emissions by burning fossil fuels to achieve the very high temperatures required for this chemical process to occur. The result is that for every tonne of steel produced this way, approximately 2 tonnes of CO2e are released into the atmosphere. 
Solution 1: 
Make greater use of scrap steel and steel slag, reducing the need to purify more iron to create steel products. (See TataSteel case studies.) This approach aligns with the 'Avoid' principal, making it a very efficient way to directly reduce emissions. The amount of emissions that can be eliminated in this way will vary. A 2022 University of Michigan study suggests that by 2050, up to 80% of steel manufacturing could be replaced by reusing steel and by using scrap steel. 
Solution 2: 
Use molten oxide electrolysis to break the iron- oxygen bond rather than carbon. This is an electricity-based technology which, when using green electricity eliminates both types of emissions from the traditional steel-making process. Their technology is scheduled to become a commercially available  in 2025. (See the Bolting Steel (https://www.bostonmetal.com/) case study.) If you are going to model this, don't start using the technology for 5-8 years to allow the system to become proven. 

Further research:
We need a better understanding of which source of emissions is addressed by reducing the use of coke and replacing it with green hydrogen. (That doesn't sound right to me. I think coke has to do with the chemical reaction and H2 has to do with the energy source.) We also need to understand how much electric arc furnaces can achieve, if anything. And we need a better understanding of how much each of these changes can achieve.

action_name: Reduce demand for long-distance shipping
Decrease high-carbon intensity foods at high-volume cafeterias
description:
Livestock farming is estimated to produced 14.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions. This comes from methane from animal digestion, nitrous oxide from manure, and carbon dioxide from land use changes for grazing and feed production. 
These are scope 3, or consumption-based emissions rather than direct emissions. So reducing these emissions cannot be reflected in a 'direct emissions inventory' like the standard GPC inventory we produce. However due to the fact that livestock farming produces such a large amount of global emissions, this is an important measure. Clients who are interested in including more of these scope 3 emissions should be encouraged to focus on opportunities like the following, which was calculated for CMCOG: 

- In a context in which 500,000 meals are served at schools, universities, hospitals and other institutions each week, implement a one-day a week (20% reduction) change to meat-free meals for all of these locations, for every year of the LCS scenario.
The calculation and assumptions used for CMCOG was as follows:
1. For every pound of meat avoided in meals, 6.514 kg CO2e are avoided. (Source: Goldstein, B.P., Pelton, R.E.O., Gounaridis, D. et al. "The carbon hoofprint of cities is shaped by geography and production in the livestock supply chain." Nat. Clim. Chang. 15, 1190–1197 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-025-02450-7
2. Currently, one week of meals at these locations serve 0.75 lbs of meat. (Source: K-12 students in the U.S. are currently served 0.75 lbs of meat per week. https://www.fns.usda.gov/school-meals/nutrition-standards/nslp-meal-pattern 
3. Therefore, estimated GHG impact = 
           (52*100000)meals/yr*0.125lbs meat/meal *6.514kg CO2e/lb meat =         
            4.2341e6 kg / year >> 4,234metric tons CO2e / year

action_name: Reduce scope 3 emissions resulting from high emissions procurement practices.
description: This action encompasses a number of specific actions a corporate or city client can take to reduce the emissions required to make or transport items and services they procure.  Establishing policies to buy locally, buy recycled, and not buy one-time use products demonstrates leadership and stimulates 'zero emissions' product and service practices in the community.

action_name: Decarbonize ocean shipping
description: In 2021, global, maritime shipping accounted for 3% of all global emissions. Yet the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has escaped much scrutiny about emissions until 2021. It was 2025 that the first carbon credit trading system was agreed to by a majority of member countries of the IMO. This system will go into effect in 2028, and is expected to decrease maritime emissions by 8% by 2030. This is much less than is required, and is a much weaker version of the initial proposal to charge ships a levy based on their emissions, and then direct those funds to the world’s most vulnerable nations to help them adapt to climate change.
